newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - IBP says Foodbrands neutral to '97 net. [corrected 16:43 gmt]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - IBP says Foodbrands neutral to '97 net. [corrected 16:43 gmt]

text.p: Meat processor IBP Inc said Wednesday its $640 million proposed acquisition of Foodbrands America Inc will be neutral to 1997 earnings, but will be accretive in 1998 and 1999.

"We believe that in 1997 it will be fundamentally a break-even proposition as it relates to (IBP's earnings)," Larry Shipley, IBP's executive vice president, corporate developement, said in a telephone interview. "In 1998 and 1999 (Corrects year from 1997), it will be accretive."
IBP bid $23.40 a share for Foodbrands.
While IBP may be able to reap some cost savings -- such as single sourcing linerboard and other packaging for both IBP and Foodbrands -- the focus is not on synergies, Shipley said.
"This is a growth story and a new platform," he noted.

Foodbrands, based in Oklahoma City, distributes frozen and refrigerated products to the growing away-from-home food preparation market. Its products include pizza toppings and crusts, frozen stuffed pastas, soups, sauces and side dishes.
IBP has made its own moves into further value-added products including trimmed and cooked meats.
"I would expect that by the year 2000, somewhere between eight and 12 percent of IBP's sales and revenues would be accounted for by these value-added products," Shipley said.
In 1996, IBP's net sales amounted to $12.54 billion and its net income was $198.7 million or $2.06 a share.
"It moves them up the value chain to add value to their commodity products," Natwest analyst David Nelson said of the deal. "So it's clearly a good move strategically."
However, Nelson said he thinks the purchase price is expensive, based on Foodbrands' 1996 income from continuing operations of $15.9 million.
Piper Jaffray analyst George Dahlman said he thought Foodbrands, which closed Tuesday at 15-3/4, had been undervalued, adding IBP's bid was "a good price."

In the near-term, the foodservice business will not completely offset the cyclicality IBP experiences in its beef and pork operations. But the Nebraska-based meat processor continues to focus on more value-added, branded products that carry a premium price, analysts said.
"What Tyson is to chicken, IBP hopes to be to beef and pork," Prudential analyst John McMillin said, referring to Tyson Foods Inc, the chicken processor that sells branded fresh and cooked poultry.
Shipley said the Foodbrands deal is aimed at capitalizing on the growing amount of meals prepared away from home, which account for more than 50 percent of total food purchases.

After the acquisition, which is expected to close in the second quarter of calendar 1997, Foodbrands will operate as an independent unit, Shipley said. Foodbrands Chairman Randolph "Randy" Devening will stay on to run that operation, he added.
IBP shares in the late morning were up 1/8 at 25-1/8, while Foodbrands was up 7-3/8 at 23-1/8.
